sentences.text: Night one.
The store intercom says your name.
You are the only person in the building.
It is seven past three in the morning, and you are shelving tins in aisle 5.
Then the front doors slide open by themselves.
A man is standing there, a regular, here every night at three.
Tonight he does not buy his paper and his coffee.
He just stands and stares, one fist clenched around something small.
The doors keep trying to close on him, and he keeps blocking them.
Rhea, the night manager, drives him back outside with a shopping cart and turns the lock.
He bumps the glass, steps back, and bumps it again.
Up in the office, twelve cameras show the town.
On every screen, someone is running.
Rhea grabs her keys and her coat.
She presses a sealed envelope into your hand.
Do not open it before day ten, she says.
And not even then, unless you have nothing left to try.
Then she is gone, and the doors lock behind her.
It is the last human voice you will hear for twelve days.
Or so you think.
You are alone with 25,000 products and one wall of glass.
Problem one: the glass.
There is a steel roller shutter, and it needs mains power.
If the power dies first, you wind it down by hand.
So you wind it down.
It takes 35 seconds, and it roars like a freight train.
House rule one: nobody comes in.
Outside, the regular is still pressed against the steel.
In his fist, you finally see it: a small brass key, tagged with a number.
Locker twelve.
At 5:23, the power goes out.
The freezers fall silent.
From the back of the store comes a heavy clunk.
The fire exit is held shut by a magnet, and magnets need power.
You sprint the whole length of the store.
You get there too late.
The door is open, and wet footprints lead inside.
